name: Cost Structure Creep
description: Per-unit costs have quietly risen over time, eroding profit even though price and volume held steady.
formula: Profit = (Price - Variable Cost per Unit) × Volume - Fixed Costs (price, volume, and fixed costs held constant) = Profit_current vs Profit_prior
business_contexts: apparel retailer with flat sales but shrinking store-level profit
regional airline with rising fuel and maintenance cost per flight
coffee chain facing higher input costs per cup
industrial parts distributor with rising per-order fulfillment cost
electronics manufacturer with rising per-unit assembly cost
question_patterns: Why has profit declined even though revenue held steady?
How much of the profit change is driven by rising per-unit costs?
If costs had stayed at prior-period levels, what would profit be today?
What is the total dollar impact of the cost structure shift?
solution_logic: Step 1: Calculate prior profit = (price_per_unit - variable_cost_per_unit_prior) × volume - fixed_costs
Step 2: Calculate current profit = (price_per_unit - variable_cost_per_unit_current) × volume - fixed_costs
Step 3: Calculate profit delta = current profit - prior profit
key_insight: Stable revenue can mask real profit erosion — always check per-unit costs, not just totals, before concluding the business is healthy.
common_mistakes: Assuming flat revenue means flat profit
Comparing total costs instead of per-unit costs
Forgetting that price and volume are unchanged, so the entire delta is cost-driven
framework_soundbite: Flat revenue can still hide a profit problem — check per-unit costs before you diagnose.
